blocks.text: A partial derivative measures how a multivariable function changes with respect to one single input variable at a time, while every other variable involved is temporarily frozen in place. It is the direct extension of the ordinary derivative, covered in the previous lesson, to functions that depend on more than one quantity at once.

blocks.alt: A function of two variables gets one variable frozen, then differentiated with respect to the other, producing one partial derivative
blocks.caption: A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative computed with all but one variable held still.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731759-767430253.png

This is not a new kind of calculus, it is the exact same machinery from the derivatives lesson, the power rule, the sum rule, the limit definition underneath them, just applied to functions of several variables one variable at a time. Since almost every real machine learning model is a function of many parameters, this idea is unavoidable.
1. From One Variable to Many

Every function covered in the previous lesson took a single number in and produced a single number out. Real functions of interest in machine learning almost never work this way, a loss function typically depends on every single weight and bias in a model simultaneously, sometimes millions of separate inputs at once.

The question a partial derivative answers is deliberately narrow, and that narrowness is exactly its strength, how does the output change if just one of those many inputs nudges slightly, while every other input stays completely fixed.
1.1 Two Variables Is Enough to Build the Idea

This lesson mostly works with functions of exactly two variables, since two is already enough to see everything important, and it keeps the arithmetic and the geometry easy to hold in your head. Every idea here extends unchanged to functions of ten variables or ten million.
2. What a Partial Derivative Means

Consider a function f of x and y. The partial derivative of f with respect to x measures the rate of change of f as x alone nudges slightly, with y locked at whatever fixed value it currently has. Nudging y instead, with x locked, produces an entirely separate number, the partial derivative with respect to y.
These two numbers generally differ from each other, and both are needed to fully describe how f responds to small changes in its two inputs. Neither one alone tells the complete story.
3. Notation for Partial Derivatives

Partial derivatives are written with a stylized, slightly rounded d, called the partial symbol, in place of the ordinary d used for single-variable derivatives. The partial derivative of f with respect to x is written as the partial symbol f over the partial symbol x.

code.content:
# Partial derivative notation:
#   partial f / partial x   (rate of change with respect to x, y held fixed)
#   partial f / partial y   (rate of change with respect to y, x held fixed)

import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = x**2 * y + y**3
print(sp.diff(f, x))   # 2*x*y
print(sp.diff(f, y))   # x**2 + 3*y**2

blocks.text: 3.1 Subscript Notation

A shorter alternative notation writes the variable being differentiated with respect to as a small subscript directly on f, so f subscript x means the partial derivative of f with respect to x. Both notations describe the exact same computation, just with different visual shorthand.
4. Holding Other Variables Fixed: The Core Trick

The entire technique behind computing a partial derivative is a single trick, treat every variable except the one being differentiated as if it were just an ordinary constant number, then differentiate exactly as covered in the previous lesson.

This single trick is why nothing new needs to be learned mechanically here, the power rule and sum rule apply exactly as before, term by term, the only new step is deciding which variable is temporarily allowed to vary and which ones are frozen for that particular computation.

blocks.title: Frozen, not deleted
blocks.content: Holding a variable fixed does not mean removing it from the expression, a frozen variable can still appear in the result, it simply is not differentiated itself, it behaves like any other constant coefficient would.

blocks.text: 5. A Worked Two-Variable Example

Take f of x and y equals x squared times y plus 3 times y. To find the partial derivative with respect to x, treat y as a fixed constant. The term x squared times y differentiates, by the power rule, to 2 x times y, since y is just along for the ride as a constant multiplier. The term 3 y contains no x at all, so it differentiates to zero with respect to x.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = x**2 * y + 3*y
print(sp.diff(f, x))   # 2*x*y
print(sp.diff(f, y))   # x**2 + 3

blocks.text: Differentiating with respect to y instead reverses the roles, x is now the frozen constant. The term x squared times y differentiates to x squared, since x squared is just a constant coefficient multiplying y. The term 3 y differentiates to the plain constant 3.
6. Partial Derivatives as Slopes Along One Axis

Geometrically, a function of two variables describes a surface, a curved sheet floating above the flat x, y plane. Slicing that surface with a plane that holds y fixed produces an ordinary single-variable curve in x, and the partial derivative with respect to x is exactly the slope of that sliced curve at the point of interest.

Slicing instead along a plane that holds x fixed produces a different curve in y, and its slope is the partial derivative with respect to y. The same surface, sliced two different ways, produces two different curves, and two different slopes.
6.1 Why the Two Slices Usually Disagree

There is no reason to expect these two slopes to match, since they are measuring steepness along two entirely different directions across the surface, one running along the x axis, the other along the y axis. A surface can easily be steep in one direction and nearly flat in the other at the exact same point.
7. Computing Partial Derivatives with the Power and Sum Rules

Because holding other variables fixed reduces the computation to an ordinary single-variable derivative, the power rule and sum rule from the previous lesson apply term by term exactly as before, with the extra bookkeeping step of tracking which variable is currently frozen.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = 4*x**3*y**2 - 2*x*y + y**5
print(sp.diff(f, x))   # 12*x**2*y**2 - 2*y
print(sp.diff(f, y))   # 8*x**3*y - 2*x + 5*y**4

blocks.text: Each term is handled independently, matching a variable to differentiate against, applying the power rule to that variable while treating every other symbol present as a constant multiplier, then summing the term-by-term results together, exactly as the sum rule allows.
8. Partial Derivatives of Both Variables at Once

It is common to compute the partial derivative with respect to every variable of a function, not just one at a time, since most downstream uses, especially the gradient covered in the next lesson, need every single one of them together.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = x**2 + y**2
partials = [sp.diff(f, v) for v in (x, y)]
print(partials)   # [2*x, 2*y]

blocks.text: Collecting every partial derivative of a function into one ordered list is not just a bookkeeping convenience, it is precisely the definition of the gradient, the subject of the very next lesson in this module.
9. Why Machine Learning Models Need Many Partial Derivatives

A real neural network loss function depends on every single weight and bias in the model simultaneously, sometimes millions or billions of separate numbers. Training that model means figuring out how the loss responds to a small nudge in each and every one of those parameters, individually, holding all the others fixed.

That is exactly what a partial derivative computes, one number per parameter, describing how sensitive the loss is to that specific parameter alone. Without partial derivatives, there would be no principled way to know how to adjust any single weight in a network with many parameters.

code.content:
# Toy loss depending on two parameters w1 and w2
import sympy as sp
w1, w2 = sp.symbols("w1 w2")
loss = (w1 - 2)**2 + (w2 + 1)**2
print(sp.diff(loss, w1))   # 2*w1 - 4, sensitivity of the loss to w1 alone
print(sp.diff(loss, w2))   # 2*w2 + 2, sensitivity of the loss to w2 alone

blocks.text: 9.1 One Partial Derivative Per Parameter, Every Single Step

During training, this computation is not done once, it is repeated at every single training step, for every single parameter, using an automated technique built on the chain rule, covered in the very next lesson after this one, so that no one has to differentiate a million-parameter loss function by hand.
10. The Direct Connection Forward to the Gradient

The gradient, covered in full in the very next lesson in this module, is nothing more than the ordered collection of every partial derivative of a function, one entry per input variable, arranged into a single vector. Everything covered in this lesson about computing individual partial derivatives is exactly the work needed to build that vector.

blocks.title: Forward reference
blocks.content: The gradient lesson picks up immediately from here, treating a collection of partial derivatives as a single object, a vector, and showing that this vector points in the direction of steepest increase of the function, a fact with enormous consequences for optimization.

blocks.text: 11. Mixed Partial Derivatives, Briefly

It is possible to take a partial derivative of an already-computed partial derivative, differentiating first with respect to x, then differentiating that result with respect to y. This produces what is called a mixed partial derivative, and for the great majority of well behaved functions encountered in this module, the order does not matter, differentiating x then y gives the same result as differentiating y then x.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = x**2 * y**3
mixed_xy = sp.diff(sp.diff(f, x), y)
mixed_yx = sp.diff(sp.diff(f, y), x)
print(mixed_xy, mixed_yx)   # 6*x*y**2, 6*x*y**2, identical

blocks.text: This idea will resurface directly in the Hessian lesson later in this module, since the Hessian is built entirely out of second-order partial derivatives, including exactly this kind of mixed term.
12. Geometric Picture: Slicing a Surface

Picturing a two-variable function as a hilly landscape hovering over a flat map is one of the most useful mental images in this entire module. A partial derivative with respect to x describes the steepness of the hill if you walk strictly in the x direction, ignoring any steepness you would feel walking in the y direction instead.

items: Freeze y, walk along x, the slope you feel is the partial derivative with respect to x.
Freeze x, walk along y, the slope you feel is the partial derivative with respect to y.
Neither slope alone describes the full steepness of the landscape, that requires combining both, exactly what the gradient does in the next lesson.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Given f of x and y equals 3 x squared y minus x y squared plus 4 y, compute both partial derivatives and evaluate them at the point x equals 1, y equals 2.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
f = 3*x**2*y - x*y**2 + 4*y
fx = sp.diff(f, x)
fy = sp.diff(f, y)
print(fx, fy)
print(fx.subs({x: 1, y: 2}), fy.subs({x: 1, y: 2}))

blocks.content: {"headers":["Partial derivative","Expression","Value at (1, 2)"],"rows":[["With respect to x","6xy - y squared","6*1*2 - 4 = 8"],["With respect to y","3x squared - 2xy + 4","3 - 4 + 4 = 3"]]}

blocks.text: At the point (1, 2), nudging x alone increases f at a rate of 8, while nudging y alone increases f at a rate of 3, two genuinely different sensitivities, exactly the kind of information a gradient, built from both of these numbers together, needs to capture in the next lesson.
14. Practice
Before checking the answer, compute both partial derivatives of g of x and y equals x cubed minus 2 x y plus y squared, then evaluate them at x equals 2, y equals 1.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
g = x**3 - 2*x*y + y**2
print(sp.diff(g, x).subs({x: 2, y: 1}))
print(sp.diff(g, y).subs({x: 2, y: 1}))

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The partial derivative with respect to x is 3 x squared minus 2y, which at (2, 1) is 12 minus 2, equal to 10. The partial derivative with respect to y is negative 2x plus 2y, which at (2, 1) is negative 4 plus 2, equal to negative 2.

blocks.text: 14.1 A Second Exercise: Which Variable Matters More Here

Using the two partial derivative values just computed, 10 for x and negative 2 for y, decide which of the two variables has a bigger effect on g at that point, and in which direction each one pushes g if nudged slightly upward.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The partial derivative with respect to x, 10, is much larger in magnitude than the partial derivative with respect to y, negative 2, so nudging x has a far bigger effect on g at this point. A small positive nudge to x increases g, since its partial derivative is positive, while a small positive nudge to y actually decreases g slightly, since its partial derivative is negative.

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes

items: Differentiating every variable at once instead of freezing all but one, collapsing the whole point of a partial derivative.
Forgetting that a frozen variable can still appear in the final expression, it is just not itself differentiated.
Assuming the partial derivative with respect to x and the partial derivative with respect to y must be equal, they generally are not.
Mixing up plain single-variable derivative notation with partial derivative notation once more than one variable is in play.
Forgetting to specify which point a partial derivative is being evaluated at, since like ordinary derivatives, its value generally changes from point to point.

blocks.text: Nearly all of these mistakes come from applying single-variable habits to a multivariable setting without pausing to ask which variable is actually varying in a given computation. Slowing down on that single question resolves the great majority of errors here.
Key Takeaway

A partial derivative measures how a multivariable function changes with respect to one variable at a time, holding every other variable fixed, computed using exactly the power rule and sum rule from the previous lesson, applied one variable at a time. Geometrically, it is the slope of the curve produced by slicing a multivariable surface along a single direction.

Its importance in machine learning comes directly from scale, a real model has one partial derivative to compute per parameter, sometimes millions of them, and each one tells you how sensitive the loss is to that specific parameter alone. Collecting all of them into a single ordered vector is exactly the gradient, the subject of the very next lesson in this module.
